citations.analysis_notes: Despite the phonological weight of four-syllable 'persnickety'—which normally favors periphrastic 'more/most persnickety' (as in CERT-3100-209)—colloquial American journalism formed synthetic superlative 'persnicketiest' by June 1923, twelve years before the Dec. 4, 1935 Washington Evening Star occurrence ('persnicketiest audience') and well ahead of late-twentieth-century synthetic comparative 'persnicketier'. Notably, Chicago Daily Tribune fashion editor Mary O'Connor Newell (whose cursive signature byline was misread in Pass 1 as 'Mary Flourney') uses 'persnicketiest' amelioratively ('most exquisitely particular') on p. 19 (leaf n18, col. 5) for couture grosgrain ribbons.

citations.analysis_notes: Establishes the chronological priority of British non-sibilant 'pernicketily' (July 1925) among overt '-ly' manner adverbs, whereas American speakers before 1930 strongly preferred flat adverbial 'persnickety' (CERT-3100-208). Exhaustive archive checks also expose a dangerous Trap A false pre-1930 hit for '-s-' 'persnicketily': Internet Archive microfilm reel ucladailybruin14losa (leaf n466, https://archive.org/details/ucladailybruin14losa/page/n466/mode/1up, 'persnicketily tidy') carries metadata 'date: 1912'—seven years before UCLA's 1919 founding—and internal text references to Royce Hall and Westwood campus dormitories place that Daily Bruin reel in the mid-1930s.

citations.verbatim_quote: p. 1607, col. 3: 'per-nick'et-y (pẽr-nĭk'ĕt-ĭ), a. [Orig. unknown.] Finical or fussy; full of petty details; as, a pernickety person. Colloq. — per-nick'et-i-ness (-ĭ-nĕs), n. Colloq.' p. 1609: upper 'per'si'fleur' -> per-sim'mon'; lower 'per'si-flate -> persil -> per'sil'lade' -> per'si-o -> Per'sis'.
citations.linguistic_note: Resolves a crucial question in the pre-1934 Merriam-Webster record: while the 1909 Webster's New International plates finally admitted non-sibilant per-nick'et-y and per-nick'et-i-ness on p. 1607, physical inspection of BOTH decks of divided-page p. 1609 proves that sibilant persnickety was omitted not only from the upper main vocabulary (per'si'fleur' -> per-sim'mon) but also from the six-column lower-page pearl-type minor/dialect register (per'si-flate -> per'sil -> per'sil'lade' -> per'si-o -> Per'sis; also absent in 1913 Secondary-School and 1918 Collegiate editions), deferring Merriam-Webster registration until the 1934 Second Edition (a 49-year lag from 1885).
